options: Rarely a single survey answers every question.
A single survey does rarely answer every question.
Rarely does a survey answer more than one question.
Rarely does a single survey answer every question.
items.answer: Rarely does a single survey answer every question.
items.explanation: Fronted negative-frequency 'rarely' brings 'does' before the subject while leaving 'answer' in its base form.

rationales.Rarely does a single survey answer every: Fronted negative-frequency 'rarely' brings 'does' before the subject while leaving 'answer' in its base form.
rationales.Rarely a single survey answers every que: This lacks the auxiliary inversion required by the requested formal fronted pattern.
rationales.A single survey does rarely answer every: This can be grammatical but does not put the frequency word first.
rationales.Rarely does a survey answer more than on: This changes the claim from rarely answering all questions to rarely answering even two.

findings: Original did not specify formal fronting as the criterion distinguishing the options.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a style requirement from general grammaticality.
audit.levelReason: A controlled rewrite preserving logical roles.
audit.similarityNote: Frequency adjunct rather than a time limit or negative object.

items.setupText: A report lists the rise in costs but gives no cause. Focus the missing explanation, not the fact that costs rose.
items.taskText: Which sentence meets that writing goal?
options: What the report explains is why costs rose.
Why costs rose is explained in the report.
What the report does not explain is whether costs rose.
What the report does not explain is why costs rose.
items.answer: What the report does not explain is why costs rose.
items.explanation: The negative what-clause introduces the gap; the why-clause identifies the missing cause.

rationales.What the report explains is why costs ro: This turns the missing explanation into something the report provides.
rationales.Why costs rose is explained in the repor: This also claims the explanation is present.
rationales.What the report does not explain is whet: This questions the occurrence, which the setup says is established.
rationales.What the report does not explain is why: The negative what-clause introduces the gap; the why-clause identifies the missing cause.

findings: Original negative pseudo-cleft used only malformed word-order alternatives.
audit.microSkill: Negative what-cleft with an embedded why-clause
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a known event from an unexplained reason.
audit.levelReason: Maintains two levels of clause meaning in an editing task.
audit.similarityNote: Known fact versus absent explanation.

items.setupText: Applicants accepted the fee but complained that they had received very little warning. Highlight the cause of their complaint.
items.taskText: Which cleft best preserves this contrast?
options: It was the fee, not the late notice, that upset the applicants.
It was the late notice, not the fee, that upset the applicants.
It was the applicants, not the staff, that the late notice upset.
It was the late notice and the fee that upset the applicants.
items.answer: It was the late notice, not the fee, that upset the applicants.
items.explanation: The focused contrast identifies the notice as the cause and excludes the accepted fee.

rationales.It was the fee, not the late notice, tha: This reverses the source of dissatisfaction.
rationales.It was the late notice, not the fee, tha: The focused contrast identifies the notice as the cause and excludes the accepted fee.
rationales.It was the applicants, not the staff, th: This contrasts the affected people, not the possible causes, and adds an unsupported claim about staff.
rationales.It was the late notice and the fee that: This adds the fee to the complaint despite the stated acceptance.

findings: Original late-notice cleft included grammatical role changes without defining the required meaning.
audit.microSkill: Cleft focus with preserved semantic roles
audit.pedagogicalValue: Checks both the contrast and who is affected.
audit.levelReason: Chooses among close grammatical clefts.
audit.similarityNote: Cause-versus-recipient focus, not mere word-order repair.

items.setupText: A trainer says, 'Only by comparing both forms can you identify which fields have changed.'
items.taskText: What does this wording present as necessary?
options: Identifying the fields before comparing the forms.
Comparing both forms in order to identify the changed fields.
Comparing whichever one form is easier to read.
Changing the fields before either form can be compared.
items.answer: Comparing both forms in order to identify the changed fields.
items.explanation: 'Only by' restricts the route to the stated result; comparison is presented as required.

rationales.Identifying the fields before comparing: This reverses the relation between the method and the result.
rationales.Comparing whichever one form is easier t: The necessary method explicitly includes both forms.
rationales.Comparing both forms in order to identif: 'Only by' restricts the route to the stated result; comparison is presented as required.
rationales.Changing the fields before either form c: The sentence concerns detecting existing changes, not making new ones.

findings: Original only-by item used base/-ing errors as its main challenge.
audit.microSkill: Only by as a necessary method
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets a fronted method restriction.
audit.levelReason: Connects means and outcome in a longer proposition.
audit.similarityNote: Method restriction rather than a condition about eligibility.

items.setupText: The timetable became more flexible, and the payment rules became more flexible too. Shorten the second clause without changing that meaning.
items.taskText: 'The timetable became more flexible, and ___.'
options: so did the payment rules
so were the payment rules
so the payment rules did
neither did the payment rules
items.answer: so did the payment rules
items.explanation: 'Did' substitutes for 'became more flexible' and the inverted order adds another subject.

rationales.so did the payment rules: 'Did' substitutes for 'became more flexible' and the inverted order adds another subject.
rationales.so were the payment rules: 'Were' gives a state rather than repeating the change expressed by 'became'.
rationales.so the payment rules did: This order confirms an earlier claim about the rules; it does not perform the requested additive comparison.
rationales.neither did the payment rules: 'Neither' would add a negative proposition, conflicting with the two positive changes.

findings: Original 'so were the rules' could legitimately mean the rules were changed, making the rejection unsafe.
audit.microSkill: Ellipsis preserves an event rather than a state
audit.pedagogicalValue: Matches the omitted predicate and distinguishes confirmatory order.
audit.levelReason: Compares auxiliary choice, change of state, and discourse function.
audit.similarityNote: Avoids the original passive ambiguity in changed/were changed.

items.setupText: Turn 'Staff must never share passwords' into a formal rule beginning 'Under no circumstances'. Preserve the complete prohibition.
items.taskText: Which revision fits the requested rule?
options: Under some circumstances may staff share passwords.
Under no circumstances need staff share passwords.
Under no circumstances must staff refuse to share passwords.
Under no circumstances may staff share passwords.
items.answer: Under no circumstances may staff share passwords.
items.explanation: The fronted negative phrase plus inverted 'may' expresses that sharing is never permitted.

rationales.Under some circumstances may staff share: This introduces permitted exceptions and also uses unmotivated inversion after a positive phrase.
rationales.Under no circumstances need staff share: This removes an obligation to share rather than prohibiting sharing.
rationales.Under no circumstances must staff refuse: This prohibits refusal, reversing the rule's practical effect.
rationales.Under no circumstances may staff share p: The fronted negative phrase plus inverted 'may' expresses that sharing is never permitted.

findings: Original tested only modal position in a prohibition and offered little semantic discrimination.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps a prohibition distinct from optionality and a prohibition on refusal.
audit.levelReason: Formal rewriting with competing modal meanings.
audit.similarityNote: Emphasis transformation is central, not free-standing modal selection.

items.setupText: The manager checked the receipt, then approved the refund. Approval had not been given before the check. Front the time restriction in formal English.
items.taskText: Choose a rewrite that preserves the event order.
options: Only after the manager had checked the receipt was the refund approved.
Only after the refund had been approved did the manager check the receipt.
Only after had the manager checked the receipt was the refund approved.
Only after the manager had checked the receipt the refund was approved.
items.answer: Only after the manager had checked the receipt was the refund approved.
items.explanation: The after-clause keeps ordinary order; the passive main clause begins 'was the refund'.

rationales.Only after the refund had been approved: This puts approval before the check, reversing the sequence.
rationales.Only after the manager had checked the r: The after-clause keeps ordinary order; the passive main clause begins 'was the refund'.
rationales.Only after had the manager checked the r: The subordinate after-clause should not invert; the main clause does.
rationales.Only after the manager had checked the r: This preserves the facts but omits the main-clause inversion requested by formal fronting.

findings: Original incorrectly treated 'the refund only was approved' as a grammar failure rather than a possible focus placement.
audit.microSkill: Fronted time clause plus passive inversion
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves event order and puts inversion in the right clause.
audit.levelReason: Coordinates past perfect, passive structure, and clause boundaries.
audit.similarityNote: Passive result after a completed checking event.

items.setupText: A reviewer writes, 'It is the wording of the question that I find confusing, not its subject matter.'
items.taskText: Which revision preserves the focus and the reviewer's judgment?
options: What I find confusing is how the question is worded, not what it is about.
What I find confusing is what the question is about, not how it is worded.
The question is confusing because its subject matter is unfamiliar.
What makes the wording confusing is the question's difficult subject matter.
items.answer: What I find confusing is how the question is worded, not what it is about.
items.explanation: The what-cleft retains the same object of criticism while changing the cleft form.

rationales.What I find confusing is what the questi: This reverses the contrast between wording and subject matter.
rationales.The question is confusing because its su: This invents an unfamiliar-topic explanation that the reviewer excludes.
rationales.What I find confusing is how the questio: The what-cleft retains the same object of criticism while changing the cleft form.
rationales.What makes the wording confusing is the: This attributes the wording problem to the subject matter, which the original contrast sets aside.

findings: Original wording cleft used scrambled alternatives rather than a meaningful focus transformation.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves a contrast across two emphasis structures.
audit.levelReason: Rephrases noun-based focus through embedded clauses.
audit.similarityNote: Transformation between cleft types.

items.setupText: The team booked the workshop for one afternoon. Little did they realize that the repairs would take a week.
items.taskText: What does 'Little did they realize' suggest in this narrative?
options: They had not appreciated how long the repairs would take.
They knew the repairs would take only a little time.
They understood the week-long delay and planned for it.
They discovered the true duration while making the booking.
items.answer: They had not appreciated how long the repairs would take.
items.explanation: Negative 'little' foregrounds their lack of awareness, which the afternoon booking illustrates.

rationales.They had not appreciated how long the re: Negative 'little' foregrounds their lack of awareness, which the afternoon booking illustrates.
rationales.They knew the repairs would take only a: Here 'little' limits their awareness, not the duration of the repairs.
rationales.They understood the week-long delay and: The short booking and negative 'little' point to inadequate awareness.
rationales.They discovered the true duration while: The narrative contrasts the brief booking with what they did not yet appreciate.

findings: Original little-did test reduced the idiom to do-support mechanics.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies which proposition little modifies.
audit.levelReason: Narrative inference supported by a contrasting action.
audit.similarityNote: Awareness scope rather than event frequency.

items.setupText: A colleague dismisses reliability as irrelevant. You want to reject that view using a what-cleft with emphatic 'does'.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correctly formed for that goal?
options: What does matter is whether is the evidence reliable.
What does matters is whether the evidence is reliable.
What does matter is whether the evidence is reliable.
What does matter it is whether the evidence is reliable.
items.answer: What does matter is whether the evidence is reliable.
items.explanation: Emphatic 'does' is possible in the subject what-clause; the embedded question retains statement order.

rationales.What does matter is whether is the evide: The embedded whether-clause requires 'the evidence is', not question inversion.
rationales.What does matter is whether the evidence: Emphatic 'does' is possible in the subject what-clause; the embedded question retains statement order.
rationales.What does matter it is whether the evide: The what-clause is already the subject of 'is'; the extra 'it' breaks this cleft.

findings: Original falsely rejected 'What does matter most' as question-like despite grammatical emphatic do.
audit.microSkill: Emphatic subject clause plus embedded question
audit.pedagogicalValue: Allows legitimate do emphasis while controlling a second clause's order.
audit.levelReason: Two interacting clause patterns, not just a main-verb ending.
audit.similarityNote: Production integrates the construction accepted in B1.

items.setupText: A writer drafts: 'Only when did we check the totals the pattern became clear.' Keep the time restriction and repair the inversion.
items.taskText: Which repair places inversion in the correct clause?
options: Only when did we check the totals did the pattern become clear.
Only when we checked the totals did the pattern become clear.
Only when we checked the totals the pattern became clear.
Only when we did checked the totals did the pattern become clear.
items.answer: Only when we checked the totals did the pattern become clear.
items.explanation: The when-clause uses ordinary order; the main clause places 'did' before its subject.

rationales.Only when did we check the totals did th: This still inverts the subordinate when-clause unnecessarily.
rationales.Only when we checked the totals the patt: This removes the erroneous inversion but fails to add the required formal main-clause inversion.
rationales.Only when we did checked the totals did: Emphatic 'did' in the time clause would require 'check', not 'checked'.
rationales.Only when we checked the totals did the: The when-clause uses ordinary order; the main clause places 'did' before its subject.

findings: Original useful clause-boundary contrast needed a specific repair task rather than vague emphasis.
audit.microSkill: Inversion attaches to the main clause
audit.pedagogicalValue: Repairs both a misplaced inversion and an omitted one.
audit.levelReason: Requires identifying two separate clause subjects.
audit.similarityNote: An editing diagnosis rather than a fresh time paraphrase.

items.setupText: Attendance has improved and complaints have fallen. Begin with 'Not only' and keep the present perfect in both clauses.
items.taskText: Which revision satisfies both instructions?
options: Not only attendance has improved, but complaints have also fallen.
Not only has attendance improved, but have complaints also fallen.
Not only has attendance improved, but complaints have also fallen.
Not only did attendance improve, but complaints have also fallen.
items.answer: Not only has attendance improved, but complaints have also fallen.
items.explanation: The first fronted clause inverts 'has'; the clause after 'but' keeps ordinary subject-before-auxiliary order.

rationales.Not only has attendance improved, but co: The first fronted clause inverts 'has'; the clause after 'but' keeps ordinary subject-before-auxiliary order.
rationales.Not only attendance has improved, but co: The first clause lacks the inversion required after this fronted not-only phrase.
rationales.Not only has attendance improved, but ha: The second declarative clause does not inherit the first clause's inversion.
rationales.Not only did attendance improve, but com: This is possible English but changes the first clause from the requested present perfect to simple past.

findings: Original focused on first-clause form but did not distinguish tense preservation and second-clause order.
audit.microSkill: Inversion limited to the not-only clause
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents copying inversion across a coordinating conjunction.
audit.levelReason: Coordinates two perfect clauses under a constrained rewrite.
audit.similarityNote: Coordination boundary rather than a subordinate time boundary.

items.setupText: A draft reads, 'In the appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.' The writer wants an ordinary statement with mild emphasis on the acknowledgment, not a question.
items.taskText: Which revision best meets that goal?
options: In the appendix, does the author acknowledge the limitation?
In the appendix, the author does acknowledge the limitation.
Only in the appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.
In no appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.
items.answer: In the appendix, the author does acknowledge the limitation.
items.explanation: A positive location phrase does not require auxiliary inversion; stressed 'does' can remain after the subject.

rationales.In the appendix, does the author acknowl: This asks a question instead of making the requested acknowledgment.
rationales.Only in the appendix does the author ack: This adds a restriction excluding other locations; the goal does not authorize that change.
rationales.In the appendix, the author does acknowl: A positive location phrase does not require auxiliary inversion; stressed 'does' can remain after the subject.
rationales.In no appendix does the author acknowled: This negates the acknowledgment rather than emphasizing it.

findings: Original appendix item treated the issue mostly as do-form selection.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates fronting, inversion, and a restriction introduced by only.
audit.levelReason: Chooses a minimal repair while preserving communicative force.
audit.similarityNote: Positive adjunct does not trigger negative-style inversion.

items.setupText: A report says, 'So confusing was the notice that several tenants called for clarification.'
items.taskText: Which relationship does this construction express?
options: The calls made an otherwise clear notice confusing.
The notice's degree of confusion led to the calls.
The tenants called despite finding the notice clear.
The tenants could call only if the notice was clear.
items.answer: The notice's degree of confusion led to the calls.
items.explanation: Fronted 'so confusing' emphasizes degree, and the that-clause gives its result.

rationales.The notice's degree of confusion led to: Fronted 'so confusing' emphasizes degree, and the that-clause gives its result.
rationales.The tenants called despite finding the n: The report links the calls to confusion rather than to an unexpected contrast.
rationales.The tenants could call only if the notic: This invents a condition and reverses the stated description.

findings: Original included incorrect feedback about where the fronted adjective belonged.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets the degree-result relationship rather than memorizing a word order.
audit.levelReason: Formal syntax with close causal alternatives.
audit.similarityNote: Degree-driven consequence, not additive so-agreement.

items.setupText: Neither password worked. Keep 'Neither the old password nor the new code' as one subject phrase in a past-tense statement.
items.taskText: Which sentence follows the requested structure?
options: Neither did the old password nor the new code worked.
Neither the old password nor the new code did worked.
Neither the old password nor the new code worked.
Neither worked the old password nor the new code.
items.answer: Neither the old password nor the new code worked.
items.explanation: Here 'neither ... nor' joins parts of the subject; it does not introduce an inverted negative clause.

rationales.Neither did the old password nor the new: The coordinated subject does not trigger inversion, and 'did' would require 'work'.
rationales.Neither the old password nor the new cod: Emphatic 'did' cannot be followed by past-form 'worked'.
rationales.Neither worked the old password nor the: The requested coordinated subject belongs before its verb, not around it.
rationales.Neither the old password nor the new cod: Here 'neither ... nor' joins parts of the subject; it does not introduce an inverted negative clause.

findings: Original neither-password item did not clearly separate subject coordination from clause inversion.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents inversion merely because the first word is negative.
audit.levelReason: Recognizes the grammatical function of a multi-part phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Neither inside a subject contrasts with B1 clause-linking nor.

items.setupText: A planner writes, 'The schedule is not merely late; it is impossible to use.'
items.taskText: How does the second clause relate to the first?
options: It corrects the claim that the schedule is late.
It explains that lateness is the only problem.
It withdraws both criticisms as too strong.
It adds a more serious criticism without denying lateness.
items.answer: It adds a more serious criticism without denying lateness.
items.explanation: 'Not merely' accepts the first criticism as insufficient on its own and adds a stronger one.

rationales.It adds a more serious criticism without: 'Not merely' accepts the first criticism as insufficient on its own and adds a stronger one.
rationales.It corrects the claim that the schedule: 'Not merely late' does not deny that it is late.
rationales.It explains that lateness is the only pr: The second clause introduces a further problem beyond lateness.
rationales.It withdraws both criticisms as too stro: Neither clause signals a withdrawal or softening of the criticism.

findings: Original rejected grammatical 'not merely was late' on preferred-position grounds.
audit.microSkill: Not merely as an escalating addition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes rejecting a limit from rejecting the description itself.
audit.levelReason: Interprets the relation between two evaluative claims.
audit.similarityNote: Escalation rather than the neutral addition in not only.

items.setupText: A policy states, 'Only if the receipt is original will the office consider a refund.'
items.taskText: What follows from this sentence alone?
options: An original receipt is required for consideration, but does not guarantee payment.
Any original receipt guarantees that the office will pay a refund.
The office must consider a refund even with a copied receipt.
The office has already approved refunds for all original receipts.
items.answer: An original receipt is required for consideration, but does not guarantee payment.
items.explanation: The restriction concerns eligibility for consideration; it does not turn consideration into approval.

rationales.Any original receipt guarantees that the: 'Only if' marks a requirement, and 'consider' is not a promise to pay.
rationales.The office must consider a refund even w: This removes the necessary condition expressed by 'only if'.
rationales.An original receipt is required for cons: The restriction concerns eligibility for consideration; it does not turn consideration into approval.
rationales.The office has already approved refunds: The future-oriented rule reports no completed approvals.

findings: Original only-if receipt task tested auxiliary order without the conditional restriction's meaning.
audit.microSkill: Only if as necessary, not sufficient
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids turning an eligibility condition into a guaranteed outcome.
audit.levelReason: Tracks a condition and the scope of a following verb.
audit.similarityNote: Eligibility plus consideration, distinct from only-by method.

items.setupText: A witness's statement was not rejected because it was brief. It was rejected because it lacked dates. Focus the actual reason using an it-cleft.
items.taskText: Which rewrite preserves that reason contrast?
options: It was because the statement was rejected that it lacked dates.
It was because the statement was brief that it was rejected.
It was the dates, rather than the statement, that were rejected.
It was because the statement lacked dates that it was rejected.
items.answer: It was because the statement lacked dates that it was rejected.
items.explanation: The because-clause is the cleft focus and supplies the reason for rejection.

rationales.It was because the statement was rejecte: This reverses the cause and the result.
rationales.It was because the statement lacked date: The because-clause is the cleft focus and supplies the reason for rejection.
rationales.It was because the statement was brief t: This selects the explicitly excluded explanation.
rationales.It was the dates, rather than the statem: This changes what was rejected instead of explaining the rejection.

findings: Original lack-of-dates cleft offered possible literary word orders under an unspecified correctness test.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves cause and effect while emphasizing a reason.
audit.levelReason: Selects a clause focus rather than a simple noun focus.
audit.similarityNote: Because-cleft with reversed-causality distractors.

items.setupText: An announcement says, 'No longer can applications be submitted by email.'
items.taskText: Which reading is supported by 'no longer' here?
options: Email submission will become available for the first time.
Email submission is available only for a shorter period.
Email submission was available before but is unavailable now.
Email applications currently take less time to submit.
items.answer: Email submission was available before but is unavailable now.
items.explanation: 'No longer' contrasts a previous possibility with its present absence; fronting gives it emphasis.

rationales.Email submission will become available f: 'No longer' marks an ending, not a new introduction.
rationales.Email submission is available only for a: The phrase changes availability, not the length of a submission period.
rationales.Email applications currently take less t: 'Longer' is part of the negative time expression, not a duration comparison here.
rationales.Email submission was available before bu: 'No longer' contrasts a previous possibility with its present absence; fronting gives it emphasis.

findings: Original no-longer item relied only on simple modal placement.
audit.microSkill: No longer and change of state
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes cessation from duration and future introduction.
audit.levelReason: Interprets a formal passive announcement.
audit.similarityNote: Temporal change rather than never-frequency or not-until onset.

items.setupText: A draft reads, 'Only after did the researchers release the raw data the criticism become persuasive.' Repair it without changing which event preceded the other.
items.taskText: Which revision correctly distributes the two clauses?
options: Only after the criticism became persuasive did the researchers release the raw data.
Only after did the researchers release the raw data did the criticism become persuasive.
Only after the researchers did release the raw data the criticism became persuasive.
Only after the researchers released the raw data did the criticism become persuasive.
items.answer: Only after the researchers released the raw data did the criticism become persuasive.
items.explanation: The release remains in the ordinary-order after-clause; 'did' belongs in the main clause about the criticism.

rationales.Only after the researchers released the: The release remains in the ordinary-order after-clause; 'did' belongs in the main clause about the criticism.
rationales.Only after the criticism became persuasi: This is grammatical but reverses the event sequence.
rationales.Only after did the researchers release t: The main clause is repaired, but the subordinate after-clause still has inappropriate inversion.
rationales.Only after the researchers did release t: Emphatic 'did release' can be grammatical inside the after-clause, but it does not supply the required main-clause inversion.

findings: Original reused a routine only-after form test rather than a multi-clause editing decision.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes grammatical emphatic do from the inversion a different clause requires.
audit.levelReason: Repairs structure while preserving chronology and allowing a legitimate emphatic variant.
audit.similarityNote: Misplaced did must be diagnosed across two different subjects.

items.setupText: Compare (1) 'Not only the proposal but also the pilot study reduced costs' and (2) 'Not only did the proposal reduce costs; it also simplified reporting.'
items.taskText: Why does only sentence 2 use auxiliary inversion?
options: Sentence 1 lacks an auxiliary because two subjects cannot share one.
In 1, not only is inside the subject; in 2, it introduces a negative-focused clause.
Sentence 2 uses inversion because reporting happens later than cost reduction.
Sentence 1 is incorrect because every initial 'not only' requires inversion.
items.answer: In 1, not only is inside the subject; in 2, it introduces a negative-focused clause.
items.explanation: A not-only subject phrase keeps ordinary order, while fronted clausal not only triggers auxiliary inversion.

rationales.Sentence 1 lacks an auxiliary because tw: A coordinated subject can share an auxiliary; subject structure, not a ban on shared auxiliaries, explains this order.
rationales.In 1, not only is inside the subject; in: A not-only subject phrase keeps ordinary order, while fronted clausal not only triggers auxiliary inversion.
rationales.Sentence 2 uses inversion because report: The structure does not establish that chronology; inversion follows the fronted expression.
rationales.Sentence 1 is incorrect because every in: Initial position alone is insufficient: 'not only' can be part of the subject, as in 1.

findings: Original not-only proposal item repeated a basic did/base form distinction.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Bases inversion on grammatical function rather than the first words alone.
audit.levelReason: Compares two superficially similar structures and explains their different behaviour.
audit.similarityNote: Paired construction analysis, not single-clause repair.

items.setupText: Rewrite 'Such a short memo had seldom been discussed at such length' with 'Seldom' first. Preserve the past perfect passive.
items.taskText: Which rewrite meets all three requirements?
options: Seldom had such a short memo been discussed at such length.
Seldom had been such a short memo discussed at such length.
Seldom was such a short memo discussed at such length.
Seldom had such a short memo discussed at such length.
items.answer: Seldom had such a short memo been discussed at such length.
items.explanation: The first auxiliary crosses the subject while the rest of the passive perfect stays together after it.

rationales.Seldom had been such a short memo discus: Only the finite auxiliary 'had' precedes the subject; 'been discussed' follows it.
rationales.Seldom was such a short memo discussed a: This is grammatical but changes the past perfect to the simple past passive.
rationales.Seldom had such a short memo been discus: The first auxiliary crosses the subject while the rest of the passive perfect stays together after it.
rationales.Seldom had such a short memo discussed a: Omitting 'been' removes the passive, leaving the memo as an implausibly incomplete active subject.

findings: Original short-memo item used a simple perfect form rather than a demanding auxiliary-chain choice.
audit.microSkill: Inverting only the finite member of an auxiliary chain
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves both anterior time and passive voice during fronting.
audit.levelReason: Three interacting constraints in a controlled transformation.
audit.similarityNote: Past perfect passive chain rather than ordinary does inversion.

items.setupText: The policy lists permissible exceptions but does not identify the person authorized to approve them. Highlight that omission.
items.taskText: Which pseudo-cleft precisely identifies what remains unclear?
options: What the policy leaves unclear is whether any exceptions are permitted.
What the policy leaves unclear is why no exceptions may be approved.
What the policy leaves unclear is who may approve the listed exceptions.
Who may approve the listed exceptions is clearly stated in the policy.
items.answer: What the policy leaves unclear is who may approve the listed exceptions.
items.explanation: The what-cleft frames an information gap, and the embedded who-clause specifies that the missing information is the decision-maker.

rationales.What the policy leaves unclear is whethe: Permission for the listed exceptions is established; the unidentified authority is the gap.
rationales.What the policy leaves unclear is why no: This invents a blanket refusal of exceptions, contrary to the context.
rationales.Who may approve the listed exceptions is: This reverses the absence of the approval authority.
rationales.What the policy leaves unclear is who ma: The what-cleft frames an information gap, and the embedded who-clause specifies that the missing information is the decision-maker.

findings: Original policy cleft had only elementary order and agreement errors as distractors.
audit.microSkill: Information focus across two embedded questions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Targets an authority gap without changing permission into prohibition.
audit.levelReason: Differentiates adjacent policy propositions through focus.
audit.similarityNote: Unknown decision-maker rather than unknown causal explanation.

items.setupText: A: 'You reject the model's calculations, then?' B: 'It is the assumption behind the model that I find problematic.'
items.taskText: What is B primarily doing with the cleft?
options: Confirming that both the assumption and all the calculations are wrong.
Withdrawing criticism of the model as a whole.
Redirecting the criticism from the calculations to their underlying assumption.
Asking A to identify which assumption the model uses.
items.answer: Redirecting the criticism from the calculations to their underlying assumption.
items.explanation: The noun phrase in cleft focus replaces A's proposed target; it does not by itself establish that every calculation is sound.

rationales.Redirecting the criticism from the calcu: The noun phrase in cleft focus replaces A's proposed target; it does not by itself establish that every calculation is sound.
rationales.Confirming that both the assumption and: The reply identifies an assumption as the target; it does not endorse that broader verdict.
rationales.Withdrawing criticism of the model as a: B still identifies something problematic within the model.
rationales.Asking A to identify which assumption th: The declarative cleft states B's criticism rather than requesting information.

findings: Original assumption cleft used scrambled foils rather than a discourse-sensitive focus decision.
audit.microSkill: Corrective cleft without overclaiming its implications
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies the redirected target while avoiding a claim that unfocused material is proven sound.
audit.levelReason: Infers speech function from a natural exchange and limits the inference.
audit.similarityNote: Critical target shifts within one model.

items.setupText: The director said that interview notes must never leave the research team. Report the instruction with 'under no circumstances' at the start of the embedded that-clause.
items.taskText: Which version preserves the prohibition and places inversion correctly?
options: The director said that under no circumstances interview notes should leave the research team.
Under no circumstances did the director say that interview notes should leave the research team.
The director said that under no circumstances should interview notes remain within the research team.
The director said that under no circumstances should interview notes leave the research team.
items.answer: The director said that under no circumstances should interview notes leave the research team.
items.explanation: The negative adjunct belongs inside the reported clause, where 'should' precedes its subject.

rationales.The director said that under no circumst: The fronted negative adjunct requires inversion within the embedded clause in this formal construction.
The negative adjunct belongs inside the reported clause, where 'should' precedes its subject.
rationales.Under no circumstances did the director: This denies that the director made a statement; it does not report a prohibition on sharing notes.
rationales.The director said that under no circumst: This reverses the prohibited action from leaving to remaining.

findings: Original under-no-circumstances item repeated simple main-clause modal ordering.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a prohibition from a denial of the reporting event.
audit.levelReason: Tracks the scope of negation across matrix and embedded clauses.
audit.similarityNote: Embedded inversion rather than the usual independent rule sentence.

items.setupText: The archive was incomplete when the study was conducted. Its missing material still weakens the conclusion today. Use formal conditional inversion to express the unreal alternative.
items.taskText: Which sentence preserves both time references?
options: Were the conclusion stronger now, the archive would have been complete.
Had the archive been complete, the conclusion was stronger now.
Had the archive been complete, the conclusion would be stronger now.
Has the archive been complete, the conclusion would be stronger now.
items.answer: Had the archive been complete, the conclusion would be stronger now.
items.explanation: Inverted 'had ... been' sets an unreal past condition, while 'would be ... now' supplies its present consequence.

rationales.Were the conclusion stronger now, the ar: This reverses the explanatory direction, making the conclusion the condition for the archive's completeness.
rationales.Had the archive been complete, the concl: The asserted past 'was' does not express the unreal present result.
Inverted 'had ... been' sets an unreal past condition, while 'would be ... now' supplies its present consequence.
rationales.Has the archive been complete, the concl: 'Has' cannot replace past-perfect 'had' in this inverted counterfactual condition.

findings: Original wrongly described adjectival 'been complete' as passive and tested only a standard past result.
audit.microSkill: Inverted past condition with present consequence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves mixed time reference and distinguishes be plus adjective from passive voice.
audit.levelReason: Integrates formal inversion with a mixed conditional timeline.
audit.similarityNote: Current consequence of an unreal past state.

items.setupText: A committee accepts an idea as worth exploring but rejects the evidence currently offered for it. An editor prefers a compact formal contrast with 'not ... but'.
items.taskText: Which revision keeps the object contrast intact?
options: The committee rejects not the idea but the evidence offered for it.
The committee rejects the idea, but not the evidence offered for it.
The committee rejects the idea as well as the evidence offered for it.
The committee does not reject either the idea or the evidence offered for it.
items.answer: The committee rejects not the idea but the evidence offered for it.
items.explanation: Delayed 'not' is legitimate in this formal paired contrast and restricts the correction to the verb's objects.

rationales.The committee rejects the idea, but not: This reverses which object is rejected.
rationales.The committee rejects the idea as well a: This adds rejection of the idea instead of excluding it from the rejection.
rationales.The committee does not reject either the: This denies the rejection of the evidence as well as the idea.
rationales.The committee rejects not the idea but t: Delayed 'not' is legitimate in this formal paired contrast and restricts the correction to the verb's objects.

findings: Original dismissed post-verbal 'not the idea' as unnatural instead of recognizing its formal contrastive use.
audit.microSkill: Delayed not in a formal object contrast
audit.pedagogicalValue: Accepts marked but legitimate order while preserving negation scope.
audit.levelReason: Distinguishes three possible scopes within close propositions.
audit.similarityNote: A formal non-cleft contrast, avoiding repeated it-clefts.

items.setupText: The key term is defined nowhere except the revised appendix. Compare two proposed openings: 'Only the revised appendix ...' and 'Only in the revised appendix ...'.
items.taskText: Which pair completes both sentences with the intended meaning?
options: does define the term / the author does define the term
does the term define / does the author define the term
defines the term / does the author define the term
defines the term / does the author defines the term
items.answer: defines the term / does the author define the term
items.explanation: The first only-phrase is the subject; the second is a fronted location adjunct, which triggers inversion.

rationales.defines the term / does the author defin: The first only-phrase is the subject; the second is a fronted location adjunct, which triggers inversion.
rationales.does define the term / the author does d: The first can use emphatic 'does', but the second lacks the inversion required by fronted 'Only in'.
rationales.does the term define / does the author d: The first reverses the grammatical roles and does not make the appendix the defining source.
rationales.defines the term / does the author defin: The second incorrectly puts an -s form after 'does'.

findings: Original appendix item duplicated only-in inversion without contrasting the nearby subject construction.
audit.microSkill: Function of an only-phrase controls inversion
audit.pedagogicalValue: Checks structure in two equivalent but differently organized statements.
audit.levelReason: Coordinates meaning equivalence with contrasting grammatical functions.
audit.similarityNote: Paired subject and location realizations of one restriction.

items.setupText: The authors avoided broad claims because their sample was very small. Rewrite with 'Such' first, retaining that cause-result relationship.
items.taskText: Which revision satisfies the requested construction?
options: Such small was the sample that the authors avoided broad claims.
Such was the authors' caution that the small sample was not used to support broad claims.
Such was the sample's small size although the authors avoided broad claims.
Such was the small size of the sample that the authors avoided broad claims.
items.answer: Such was the small size of the sample that the authors avoided broad claims.
items.explanation: 'Such was + noun phrase' foregrounds degree; the that-clause gives the resulting restraint.

rationales.Such small was the sample that the autho: An adjective alone takes the pattern 'So small was ...'; 'such' here needs a noun phrase or the 'such was' construction.
rationales.Such was the small size of the sample th: 'Such was + noun phrase' foregrounds degree; the that-clause gives the resulting restraint.
rationales.Such was the authors' caution that the s: This makes the authors' degree of caution the cause instead of preserving the stated cause, the sample's small size.
rationales.Such was the sample's small size althoug: 'Although' substitutes concession for the requested degree-result relationship.

findings: Original so-limited item repeated adjective/be order without testing the related such construction.
audit.microSkill: Such inversion with a noun-based degree expression
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes so plus adjective from such plus nominal degree.
audit.levelReason: Transforms syntax and checks the relation of the following clause.
audit.similarityNote: Noun-based degree fronting rather than B2's interpretation of so.

items.setupText: A project diary says, 'No sooner had the funding been approved than the timetable changed.'
items.taskText: Which conclusion is warranted by this construction alone?
options: The timetable changed before approval and caused it to be granted.
The timetable had to change as a condition of receiving approval.
The timetable changed almost immediately after approval.
The approval and timetable change are presented as exactly simultaneous.
items.answer: The timetable changed almost immediately after approval.
items.explanation: 'No sooner ... than' emphasizes near-immediate succession, but timing alone does not state causation.

rationales.The timetable changed before approval an: This reverses the temporal sequence and adds an unsupported cause.
rationales.The timetable had to change as a conditi: The construction presents two closely timed events, not a condition attached to approval.
rationales.The timetable changed almost immediately: 'No sooner ... than' emphasizes near-immediate succession, but timing alone does not state causation.
rationales.The approval and timetable change are pr: The construction orders one event just after another rather than asserting exact simultaneity.

findings: Original no-sooner task reduced an advanced construction to helper and conjunction errors.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Limits conclusions to what the temporal construction actually conveys.
audit.levelReason: Distinguishes temporal ordering, conditions, and causality.
audit.similarityNote: Inference boundary rather than choosing than mechanically.

items.setupText: A: 'But we do have the data.' B: 'The issue is not whether the data exist, but whether we can use them.'
items.taskText: What does B's parallel contrast do in this exchange?
options: It concedes that the data do not exist.
Moves the discussion from possession of data to their usability.
It states that existing data must therefore be usable.
It replaces a question about usability with one about existence.
items.answer: Moves the discussion from possession of data to their usability.
items.explanation: The paired whether-clauses reject A's proposed issue as insufficient and identify the relevant question.

B sets existence aside rather than denying it.
rationales.It states that existing data must theref: B distinguishes existence from usability instead of treating the former as proof of the latter.
rationales.It replaces a question about usability w: This reverses the direction of B's shift.
rationales.Moves the discussion from possession of: The paired whether-clauses reject A's proposed issue as insufficient and identify the relevant question.

findings: Original not-whether contrast used mostly scrambled placement rather than argumentative meaning.
audit.microSkill: Parallel interrogative clauses redefine an issue
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes a shift in the question under discussion without inventing an answer to it.
audit.levelReason: Interprets a discourse move between related propositions.
audit.similarityNote: The focus is a question, not an asserted alternative fact.

items.setupText: Compare 'Little of the archive survived' and 'Little did the reviewers know about the missing files.'
items.taskText: Which explanation correctly accounts for the different word orders?
options: The first sentence is wrong because every fronted 'little' requires 'did'.
Little is part of the subject in 1 but a negative adverbial in 2.
The second sentence is a direct question because did precedes reviewers.
The difference is that survived is past but know is present.
items.answer: Little is part of the subject in 1 but a negative adverbial in 2.
items.explanation: A negative-quantity subject keeps ordinary order, whereas fronted negative 'little' as an adverbial calls for auxiliary inversion.

rationales.Little is part of the subject in 1 but a: A negative-quantity subject keeps ordinary order, whereas fronted negative 'little' as an adverbial calls for auxiliary inversion.
rationales.The first sentence is wrong because ever: 'Little of the archive' is a complete subject and does not require inversion.
rationales.The second sentence is a direct question: Fronted negative expressions can produce inversion in declarative statements as well as questions.
rationales.The difference is that survived is past: The second sentence is also past; 'did' carries its tense.

findings: Original little-reviewers item repeated did ordering without addressing the function of little.
audit.microSkill: Negative quantity subject versus negative adverbial
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains why identical opening words can permit different orders.
audit.levelReason: Requires structural classification and tense interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Little has two grammatical functions, unlike a single idiomatic narrative.

items.setupText: An analyst writes, 'It was not because the baseline shifted that the comparison failed; the two groups had been measured differently.'
items.taskText: What does this wording deny?
options: That the baseline shifted at all.
That the comparison failed.
That the groups were measured differently.
That a shifted baseline caused the comparison's failure.
items.answer: That a shifted baseline caused the comparison's failure.
items.explanation: Negation targets the because-clause as an explanation, while the following clause offers a different cause.

The cleft negates the proposed reason; it does not settle whether the baseline changed.
rationales.That a shifted baseline caused the compa: Negation targets the because-clause as an explanation, while the following clause offers a different cause.
The failure is treated as the event requiring explanation, not denied.
rationales.That the groups were measured differentl: The final clause asserts that difference as the alternative explanation.

findings: Original because-cleft tested basic word order rather than the scope of a reason-focused cleft.
audit.microSkill: Negated reason cleft versus negated event
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps denial of causality separate from denial of either event.
audit.levelReason: Tracks negation over a causal relation and its alternatives.
audit.similarityNote: Denies a relationship rather than simply substituting an affirmative reason.

items.setupText: Use 'Not a single applicant' first in two sentences: one says nobody received an explanation; the other says the manager consulted nobody.
items.taskText: Which pair preserves both meanings and uses formal standard order?
options: Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant did the manager consult.
Not a single applicant did receive an explanation. / Not a single applicant the manager consulted.
Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant consulted the manager.
Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant did consult the manager.
items.answer: Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant did the manager consult.
items.explanation: The negative subject in the first stays before its verb; the fronted negative object in the second triggers 'did the manager consult'.

rationales.Not a single applicant did receive an ex: The first can be emphatic, but the second fronted negative object requires inversion in the requested formal style.
rationales.Not a single applicant received an expla: The second makes applicants the consulting agents rather than the people whom the manager did not consult.
The negative subject in the first stays before its verb; the fronted negative object in the second triggers 'did the manager consult'.
The second again makes the applicant the subject; emphatic 'did' does not preserve the manager's role.

findings: Original not-a-single item was primarily basic article and singular agreement testing at C1.
audit.microSkill: Negative subject versus fronted negative object
audit.pedagogicalValue: Determines inversion from syntactic role while preserving agent and recipient.
audit.levelReason: Compares two superficially identical openings across different argument structures.
audit.similarityNote: Negative object fronting introduces a distinct inversion trigger.

items.setupText: The estimate cannot be trusted unless its limitation is disclosed. Rewrite with 'Only if' first, preserving the requirement without promising that disclosure alone makes the estimate trustworthy.
items.taskText: Which formal rewrite preserves that logical restriction?
options: Only if the estimate can be trusted is the limitation disclosed.
Only if the limitation is disclosed can the estimate be trusted.
If the limitation is disclosed, the estimate can be trusted.
Only if the limitation is not disclosed can the estimate be trusted.
items.answer: Only if the limitation is disclosed can the estimate be trusted.
items.explanation: The fronted condition remains necessary for trust; the main clause inverts 'can' without making disclosure sufficient.

rationales.Only if the limitation is disclosed can: The fronted condition remains necessary for trust; the main clause inverts 'can' without making disclosure sufficient.
rationales.Only if the estimate can be trusted is t: This makes trust a requirement for disclosure, reversing the implication.
rationales.If the limitation is disclosed, the esti: This presents disclosure as sufficient, whereas the original only made it necessary.
rationales.Only if the limitation is not disclosed: This makes non-disclosure the condition, contradicting the original restriction.

findings: Original only-if estimate item relied solely on misplaced auxiliaries.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves implication direction during an emphasis rewrite.
audit.levelReason: A formal transformation with close but logically different alternatives.
audit.similarityNote: Equivalence editing, beyond B2's interpretation of an eligibility rule.

items.setupText: An editor wants to put the rejected priority first while preserving 'The report emphasizes accuracy rather than speed.'
items.taskText: Which revision follows that focus instruction without adding a new claim?
options: Rather than speed, the report emphasizes accuracy.
Rather than accuracy, the report emphasizes speed.
Only when speed increases does the report emphasize accuracy.
Not only speed but also accuracy is emphasized in the report.
items.answer: Rather than speed, the report emphasizes accuracy.
items.explanation: The contrasting phrase can be fronted without auxiliary inversion; it places the rejected priority first.

rationales.Rather than accuracy, the report emphasi: This reverses which priority is accepted and which is rejected.
rationales.Rather than speed, the report emphasizes: The contrasting phrase can be fronted without auxiliary inversion; it places the rejected priority first.
rationales.Only when speed increases does the repor: This introduces a time condition absent from the source.
rationales.Not only speed but also accuracy is emph: This changes a preference contrast into additive emphasis on both priorities.

findings: Original rather-than item used elementary scrambled alternatives despite its C1 label.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves a preference while distinguishing it from addition and conditional restriction.
audit.levelReason: Controls information order and propositional content together.
audit.similarityNote: Fronted rather-than phrase is not a negative inversion trigger.

items.setupText: The hearing had barely begun when the recording failed. An editor proposes using 'Scarcely' first while retaining the original sequence and passive-free wording.
items.taskText: Which revision accurately carries out the proposal?
options: Scarcely had the hearing begun when the recording failed.
Scarcely had the recording failed when the hearing began.
Scarcely had the hearing been begun when the recording failed.
Scarcely the hearing had begun when the recording failed.
items.answer: Scarcely had the hearing begun when the recording failed.
items.explanation: 'Scarcely had' preserves the earlier, barely begun event; 'when' introduces the interruption.

rationales.Scarcely had the recording failed when t: This swaps the closely sequenced events.
rationales.Scarcely had the hearing been begun when: This introduces a passive reading and an implied agent, which the instruction excludes.
rationales.Scarcely the hearing had begun when the: The fronted negative adverb requires auxiliary-before-subject order in this formal pattern.
rationales.Scarcely had the hearing begun when the: 'Scarcely had' preserves the earlier, barely begun event; 'when' introduces the interruption.

findings: Original hearing item repeated no-sooner-style form foils and lacked a concrete editing goal.
audit.microSkill: Scarcely fronting preserves aspect and event order
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a grammatical voice change from an equivalent rewrite.
audit.levelReason: Maintains timeline, voice, and formal word order simultaneously.
audit.similarityNote: An interrupted onset, not a causal claim about immediate succession.

items.setupText: Compare 'What the witness did was repeat the warning' and 'What the witness did was to repeat the warning.'
items.taskText: Which editorial judgment is accurate?
options: Only the first is grammatical because did forbids to anywhere later.
Both are grammatical, with no change in the reported action.
Only the second is grammatical because every complement of was needs to.
Both are grammatical, but only the second says the warning was actually repeated.
items.answer: Both are grammatical, with no change in the reported action.
items.explanation: The do-pseudo-cleft permits both a bare infinitive and a to-infinitive without changing who repeated the warning.

rationales.Only the first is grammatical because di: The 'to' is in the focused complement after 'was', not directly after auxiliary 'did'.
rationales.Only the second is grammatical because e: A bare infinitive is also allowed in this do-pseudo-cleft, and many other complements of be are not infinitives.
rationales.Both are grammatical, with no change in: The do-pseudo-cleft permits both a bare infinitive and a to-infinitive without changing who repeated the warning.
rationales.Both are grammatical, but only the secon: Both identify repeating the warning as what the witness did; the extra 'to' does not change actuality.

findings: Original witness what-cleft was another basic order/agreement question at C1.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids inventing a meaning or correctness distinction between legitimate variants.
audit.levelReason: Evaluates a construction-specific alternation and its semantic limits.
audit.similarityNote: Cleft licensing is central; not another verb-pattern drill from the gerunds topic.

items.setupText: A reviewer writes, 'Nowhere in the published policy does it say that late appeals are automatic.'
items.taskText: Which conclusion is justified by that sentence alone?
options: Late appeals are expressly prohibited by the published policy.
Late appeals cannot be approved by any route.
The policy promises that each late appeal will be considered individually.
The published policy contains no statement granting automatic late appeals.
items.answer: The published policy contains no statement granting automatic late appeals.
items.explanation: 'Nowhere in' restricts the negative claim to what this document says.

rationales.Late appeals are expressly prohibited by: Absence of an automatic-appeal statement is not an express prohibition on appeals.
rationales.The published policy contains no stateme: 'Nowhere in' restricts the negative claim to what this document says.
rationales.Late appeals cannot be approved by any r: The sentence makes no claim about every possible approval route.
rationales.The policy promises that each late appea: An individual-review promise cannot be inferred from the absence of an automatic-appeal provision.

findings: Original nowhere-policy item tested routine does placement rather than the limited evidential claim.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes absence of a statement from a substantive prohibition or promise.
audit.levelReason: Limits an inference to the scope of the fronted source phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Negative textual evidence rather than a rule imposing a prohibition.

items.setupText: An analyst writes, 'Only by treating silence as ambiguous can we avoid taking every unanswered request as consent.'
items.taskText: Which interpretation respects both the fronted restriction and 'every'?
options: Treating silence as ambiguous is presented as necessary to avoid a blanket inference of consent.
The analyst requires every unanswered request to be treated as a refusal.
Treating silence as ambiguous guarantees that no unanswered request can involve consent.
The analyst says that consent must be assumed unless every request receives an answer.
items.answer: Treating silence as ambiguous is presented as necessary to avoid a blanket inference of consent.
items.explanation: 'Only by' specifies a necessary approach; the avoided inference applies consent to every unanswered request, not merely some.

rationales.The analyst requires every unanswered re: Rejecting a blanket inference of consent does not turn silence into a blanket refusal.
rationales.Treating silence as ambiguous is present: 'Only by' specifies a necessary approach; the avoided inference applies consent to every unanswered request, not merely some.
rationales.Treating silence as ambiguous guarantees: The sentence neither makes the method sufficient for every decision nor excludes consent in particular cases.
rationales.The analyst says that consent must be as: This changes the condition from how silence is interpreted to whether every request is answered.

findings: Original C2 only-by item used elementary -ing and inversion errors beneath legal vocabulary.
audit.microSkill: Method restriction combined with quantifier scope
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves necessity without converting rejection of a universal inference into a universal opposite.
audit.levelReason: Tracks restriction, negation, and universal quantification together.
audit.similarityNote: Nested universal claim distinguishes this from simpler only-by items.

items.setupText: Reviewing today's interpretation, an editor writes, 'Not since the 1998 amendment has the clause been read so narrowly.'
items.taskText: Which reading is best supported by the sentence in this context?
options: No one has interpreted the clause at all since the amendment.
The clause was first read narrowly in 1998 and has become narrower every year.
Today's reading is necessarily narrower than the reading made at the time of the amendment.
Today's reading reaches a degree of narrowness not matched in the intervening period.
items.answer: Today's reading reaches a degree of narrowness not matched in the intervening period.
items.explanation: The not-since construction presents the current reading as exceptional relative to the period after that earlier benchmark.

rationales.No one has interpreted the clause at all: The restriction concerns readings this narrow, not the occurrence of any interpretation.
rationales.The clause was first read narrowly in 19: The sentence supplies a comparison point, not a year-by-year trend.
rationales.Today's reading reaches a degree of narr: The not-since construction presents the current reading as exceptional relative to the period after that earlier benchmark.
rationales.Today's reading is necessarily narrower: It need not exceed the old benchmark; the sentence says the intervening period offers no match.

findings: Original not-since clause item tested elementary perfect-passive assembly rather than its retrospective comparison.
audit.microSkill: Not-since fronting with a degree benchmark
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an unmatched interval from continuous change or a claim of historical superiority.
audit.levelReason: Integrates current focus, retrospective interval, and comparative degree.
audit.similarityNote: An exceptional recurrence, unlike no-longer cessation or not-until onset.

items.setupText: A: 'The dissent seems to reject permission altogether.' B: 'What it rejects is the equation of permission with consent.'
items.taskText: Which account best captures B's use of focus?
options: B says the dissent regards permission and consent as interchangeable.
B narrows the target to equating permission with consent.
B proves that the dissent accepts every use of permission not involving consent.
B withdraws the claim that the dissent rejects anything relevant to consent.
items.answer: B narrows the target to equating permission with consent.
items.explanation: The focused complement identifies an equation as the rejected object; it does not by itself establish a comprehensive positive stance on permission.

rationales.B narrows the target to equating permiss: The focused complement identifies an equation as the rejected object; it does not by itself establish a comprehensive positive stance on permission.
rationales.B says the dissent regards permission an: The equation between the two is precisely what B says the dissent rejects.
rationales.B proves that the dissent accepts every: Correcting the target does not license universal approval of all remaining cases.
rationales.B withdraws the claim that the dissent r: Rejecting the equation remains directly relevant to consent, so the reply does not remove that criticism.

findings: Original dissent pseudo-cleft was a simple word-order exercise with advanced nouns.
audit.microSkill: Corrective focus and limits on implied acceptance
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes narrowing the target from endorsing everything outside it.
audit.levelReason: Interprets a discourse correction while limiting its presuppositions and implications.
audit.similarityNote: Rejection of an equivalence rather than rejection of either individual concept.

items.setupText: An editor must preserve two facts: the panel questions the reasoning, and it does not question the outcome. The record does not say that it positively endorses the outcome.
items.taskText: Which formal cleft makes the contrast without strengthening either claim?
options: It is not the outcome but the reasoning that the panel questions.
It is the outcome that the panel endorses, despite questioning the reasoning.
It is the reasoning as well as the outcome that the panel questions.
It is not the reasoning but the outcome that the panel questions.
items.answer: It is not the outcome but the reasoning that the panel questions.
items.explanation: The negated and affirmative focus phrases preserve the two targets without upgrading non-objection into endorsement.

rationales.It is the outcome that the panel endorse: Positive endorsement is stronger than the recorded absence of a challenge.
rationales.It is the reasoning as well as the outco: This adds a challenge to the outcome, contrary to the record.
rationales.It is not the reasoning but the outcome: This reverses the two objects of the contrast.
rationales.It is not the outcome but the reasoning: The negated and affirmative focus phrases preserve the two targets without upgrading non-objection into endorsement.

findings: Original outcome/reasoning cleft offered mainly malformed negation positions.
audit.pedagogicalValue: Protects the distinction between not challenging and endorsing.
audit.levelReason: Precise editing must retain both contrast and evidential strength.
audit.similarityNote: An explicit record-preservation task, not an inference setup that gives away an answer.

items.setupText: A writer says, 'If they had not intended court proceedings, the wording would have been different.' Front the counterfactual condition without 'if', preserving its negative form and time reference.
items.taskText: Which revision expresses that supplied counterfactual in formal standard English?
options: Had not they intended court proceedings, the wording would have been different.
Had they not intended court proceedings, the wording would have been different.
Had they intended court proceedings, the wording would not have been different.
Were they not to intend court proceedings, the wording would have been different.
items.answer: Had they not intended court proceedings, the wording would have been different.
items.explanation: Only 'had' moves before the subject; 'not intended' remains after it, preserving the negative past condition.

rationales.Had not they intended court proceedings,: In this uncontracted conditional inversion, the subject precedes 'not': 'Had they not intended'.
rationales.Had they not intended court proceedings,: Only 'had' moves before the subject; 'not intended' remains after it, preserving the negative past condition.
rationales.Had they intended court proceedings, the: This shifts negation from the condition to the consequence and is not equivalent to the supplied counterfactual.
rationales.Were they not to intend court proceeding: This uses a prospective hypothetical condition instead of the supplied unreal past intention.

findings: Original arbitration conditional used basic participle and if-plus-inversion foils.
audit.microSkill: Negative conditional inversion with preserved scope and time
audit.pedagogicalValue: Places uncontracted not after the subject while distinguishing logical and temporal rewrites.
audit.levelReason: Coordinates inversion, negative scope, and counterfactual time.
audit.similarityNote: Negative condition, unlike C1's affirmative mixed-time archive condition.

items.setupText: A journal's style editor wants an emphatic degree-result sentence. The source says that the links between cause and effect were too weak to support the conclusion, not that no links existed.
items.taskText: Which revision adds the requested emphasis without overstating the evidence?
options: So weak were the links between cause and effect that the conclusion was shown to be false.
So weak were the links between cause and effect that they could not support the conclusion.
Weak though the links between cause and effect were, they supported the conclusion.
Only because the conclusion was unsupported did the links between cause and effect become weak.
items.answer: So weak were the links between cause and effect that they could not support the conclusion.

items.setupText: The parties agree that a waiver was signed. They dispute whether the signer understood it and chose it freely. A formal summary should put 'At issue' first and preserve that unresolved question.

items.setupText: Compare 'The doctrine is not merely narrow; it is unstable' with 'The doctrine is merely not narrow; that alone tells us little.'
